units: fear has an identifiable trigger
fear stops once the danger has passed
anxiety is aimed at a future and uncertain danger
anxiety shows itself through muscular tension and damp hands
fear is compared to a brief warning signal
anxiety is compared to a faulty warning signal that never stops
both emotions begin as a form of protection
telling the two states apart helps you respond in a fitting way
text: You are walking down a dim corridor and a door slams behind you. Your heart bolts, your shoulders lock, a chill runs down the back of your neck. That is fear. Something set it off, you know what, and it drains away the moment the threat has passed. Anxiety runs on a different clock. Nothing solid stands in front of it; it leans forward instead, towards whatever might come. You feel it as a clenched jaw, as damp palms that stay damp for no reason you can name. Fear is an alarm that rings and then stops. Anxiety is an alarm wired badly, humming away under everything else. Both of them began as ways of keeping you safe. What separates them is how long they last and what they point at. Once you can put a name to whichever one has hold of you, you are already picking a better answer.

units: adults gather every week in a room used for stage work
the workshop is meant for people whom speaking in public shuts down
the woman who runs it worked in care beforehand
the session is built round three families of exercises
the first set of exercises works on the breath
the second set works on the expressions of the face
the third set consists of looking at one another in silence
this wordless face-to-face often brings on a burst of laughter
the woman who runs it reads that laughter as a release
text: A handful of adults gather once a week in a rehearsal room with scuffed, splintered floorboards. The workshop is meant for people whom speaking in public shuts down completely. The woman who runs it trained in care work before she turned to directing, and she builds each session round three families of exercises. The first work on breath: draw the air in, hold it, let it go on a long sigh, until the throat loosens. The second work on the face: pull a grimace, keep it, drop it, so you feel the difference between tension that happens to you and tension you choose. The last work on the eyes: two people hold each other's gaze without speaking, and one of them nearly always ends up laughing. That laugh is no failure, she says. It marks the moment a grip of awkwardness lets go.

units: the first step is to settle somewhere nobody is asking anything of you
you put your hands on your legs and breathe without forcing
the next step asks you to find where anger shows in the body
you are advised to name that place silently
you then loosen the joints one after another
each loosening goes with a whole breath
you wait until the intensity falls back on its own
the last step is to say briefly what you were trying to protect
that need is most often the need to be heard
text: Begin by sitting where nobody is asking anything of you. Lay your palms flat on your thighs and let the air sink as far as your belly, without pushing it along. Then look for the exact spot where anger has settled: a heat climbing into the cheeks, a tightness under the ribs, a stiffness in the fists. Name that spot silently, the way you name the rooms of a house you are seeing for the first time. Now loosen one joint after another, the jaw, the neck, the fingers, giving each of them a whole breath. Wait for the wave to fall back of its own accord; it does fall back, though it takes the route it wants. Last of all, say quietly, out loud, the shortest sentence that describes what you were defending. More often than not it was no insult to avenge and no argument to win, but a need to be heard.

units: volunteers were kept awake through a whole night
the study pairs brain imaging with a measure of sweating
the brain structure that detects threat becomes more reactive
its reaction lasts longer than it ordinarily would
the cause put forward is a weakened control by the frontal region
frontal activity drops as the sleep debt builds
the participants take faces without expression for threatening ones
they react sharply to sounds of low intensity
the irritability produced spoils the following night and restarts the loop
text: A research team has just set out the measurements taken from volunteers who were kept awake for a whole night without a break. The protocol pairs brain imaging with readings of the sweat carried on the skin. What the loss of sleep reaches first is the deep structure that weighs up threat: it fires harder, and above all for far longer, in front of images that are perfectly ordinary. Behind that lies a slackening of the control the frontal region exerts, an activity that falls away steadily as the sleep debt builds. The behaviour then shows it plainly enough. Volunteers take blank faces for hostile ones, they flinch at faint sounds, and they report a damp grip in the hands that outlasts the session. The authors close on a loop that feeds itself: the irritability piled up spoils the night that follows, and round it goes again.

units: the waiting area was set in a cramped passage
the seats stood facing one another in two rows
a swing door made unpredictable bangs
the ceiling light was dull
people left the place more tense than they came in
the seats were regrouped into clusters turned towards the windows
a soft floor covering was laid to soak up the noise
a fitting was added to the door to stop the banging
the expected wait is now shown on display
signs of irritation have fallen since then
text: The waiting area of the department occupied a narrow passage, furnished with seats set out in two rows that faced one another. There was no escaping another person's gaze; a swing door banged at moments nobody could predict; the fitting overhead shed a dull, colourless light. People came in tense and walked out tighter still. The nursing team therefore reworked the whole layout. The rows were broken up into clusters angled towards the windows, a soft covering was laid over the floor to soak up the sound of footsteps, and the door was given a damper. A panel on the wall now shows how long the wait is expected to be, which takes away the least bearable part of it, the not knowing. Since then the staff report a clear drop in gestures of annoyance, and a calmer response whenever an appointment runs late.

units: the text sets a digital tracking tool against an exchange with a professional
the human exchange rests on a living relationship
the professional picks up signs the patient does not put into words
the digital tool catches neither the wavering of a voice nor the silences
the tool stores ratings in the form of data
the strength of the tool is the reliability of what it keeps
human memory warps memories and smooths them flat
the tool can bring out a pattern that went unnoticed
the writer holds that the two approaches fill separate roles
text: Should you hand your moods over to a logging app? The question deserves better than the flat answers it tends to attract. A session with a practitioner rests on a living relationship: the voice falters, a sigh slips out, and the person opposite picks up what the account leaves unsaid. Automated tracking hears none of that, neither the wobble in a voice nor the awkward pause; it stores ticked boxes and curves. Its strength sits elsewhere. It keeps a faithful record, where remembering warps things and smooths them flat. Someone certain of having felt low for weeks opens the log and finds a pattern he had never noticed. So the two do not stand in the same place. The log measures and reminds; the session interprets and walks alongside. To set them against each other is to choose between a scale and a gaze.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: she takes calls on a night-time telephone line
her post sits in a room with no window
she has held the job for a great many seasons
she names three qualities the role calls for
the first is to bear the silences of the callers
the second is to catch the audible signs of distress
the third is to let go once the shift is over
she walks home to shed what she has heard
a caller apologised for ringing about something small
she told him that something small deserved the same attention
text: She takes the calls that come in on a helpline late into the night, in a room with no window at all, and she has been doing it for a great many seasons now. Three things make the job, she says, laughing. Patience first of all: she lets a silence run on and on, because a caller in tears needs someone who will not rush in to fill the gap for them. Then the ear: she catches a tremor in the voice, a breath held back, a sentence that keeps breaking off at the very same word. Last, distance: once the shift ends she walks the whole way home and leaves behind her what she has heard, or she would never last out the week. The other night, she says, a caller apologised for having bothered anyone over so little. She told him that on this line the little things had the same right to be heard as the worst of them.

units: the film opens on a long still shot of an empty seat
that opening deliberately puts the audience ill at ease
the first part follows a family through the weeks after a death
that part carries no narration and no added soundtrack
specialists on grief speak in the middle part
the reviewer judges that those contributions weaken the film
the closing part goes back to the silence of the opening
the scene judged the best shows two relatives holding each other without speaking
the reviewer praises the absence of sentimentality
text: The film opens on a static shot of an empty chair, held long enough to leave the audience distinctly uneasy. That choice announces everything that follows it. The first part goes with a family through the weeks after a death, with no voice-over and no music laid over the images; all you hear are the sounds of the household and, now and then, a stifled sob. The middle part shifts gear. Specialists on grief step in, and the film loses ground here, since their explanations cover over what the faces on screen had already said. The closing part picks the silence back up and delivers the truest scene of the lot: an awkward embrace between two relatives who cannot find the words. You leave the cinema flattened, and yet with the rare sense of having watched sorrow handled without a trace of indulgence.

units: the writer explains to her reader the reason for her long silence
she stopped answering after bad news
her withdrawal did not come from any lack of affection
every conversation made her go back over her pain
keeping to herself weighed on her more than the sadness did
she has taken up walking in the evening again
the questions of neighbours still make her flush
she answers all the same and it is getting easier
she asks the person she writes to to be in touch again
text: I am writing to you because my silence over these past weeks must have hurt you, and you deserve to know where it came from. After the news you know about, I stopped answering messages. It was not that I had stopped caring. Every call asked me to tell the story again, and telling it opened the same wound, so I said nothing, and keeping to myself cut me off far more surely than the grief ever did. That is what I see now: the distance, and not the sorrow, is what made me so heavy to carry. I have started going out for a walk in the evenings again. My face still burns when a neighbour asks how I am getting on, and yet I answer, and each answer costs me a little less than the one before it. Write to me whenever you feel like it. I cannot promise to be cheerful. I promise to pick up.

units: a common question asks whether slowed breathing really works
the explanation rests on a nerve linking the brain to the inner organs
lengthening the out-breath rouses that nerve
this rousing brings the heart rate down
the protocols advise a cycle longer than ordinary breathing
the out-breath must last at least as long as the in-breath
many patients give up after a first attempt that went badly
that early failure comes from breathing too deeply
the volume drawn in must be cut while the cycle is stretched
practice is advised away from moments of strain
text: One question comes up again and again in consultations: does slowing the breath truly settle anything, or is it a comforting belief? The mechanism is well established. A drawn-out out-breath rouses the nerve that runs from the brain stem to the organs of the trunk, and that rousing brings the heart rate down. Second question: what pace? The accepted protocols stretch the cycle well past its spontaneous rate, giving the out-breath a length at least equal to the in-breath. Third question: what about failure? Plenty of patients give up because the first attempt sharpens the alarm instead of quieting it. The trouble is unintended over-breathing, brought on by drawing in far too much air. The answer is to make each breath smaller while making it longer, and to rehearse in calm conditions before calling on it under strain.
